name: Simon says
description: Students act only when a command starts with Simon says.
steps: A leader gives commands: Simon says {cmds}. Students act only when the phrase starts with Simon says.
Speed up and mix the order. A student who moves by mistake becomes a helper judge, so nobody sits out.
Small groups take turns as Simon.
easier: Show the action as you say it.
harder: Use two-part commands and negatives: do not jump.

adaptations.mobility: In Simon says, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Simon says, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Simon says, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Traffic lights
description: Green, amber and red signs control how students move.
aim: Respond to colour and action commands
steps: Students move around the space. Show a colour sign: green walk, amber slow, red freeze.
Add commands to colours: green jump, amber turn, red balance on one foot.
A student holds the signs and calls the colours in English.
easier: Use only green and red.
harder: Add directions: green go left, amber go back.

adaptations.mobility: In Traffic lights, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Traffic lights, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Traffic lights, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Freeze and describe
description: Music plays, students move, then freeze when it stops.
steps: Play music while students move around. When it stops they freeze in a pose.
Point to a frozen student. The class describes the pose: She is jumping.
Add a target: freeze next to a friend, behind a cone, at the blue line.
phrases: He is next to the cone.
easier: Name the action yourself first.
harder: Ask for two sentences about each pose.

name: Mirror and command
description: One partner gives commands, the other mirrors the action.
steps: Pairs face each other. A gives a command ({cmds}). B does it like a mirror.
Add a second and third command. A links them with then.
Swap. Each pair invents a 5-command sequence for the next pair.
student: A says a command. B does it.
Swap and invent a new one.
easier: Give one command at a time.
harder: Chain five commands with then and after that.

adaptations.hearing: In Mirror and command, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Action chain
description: Each student repeats the chain of actions and adds a new one.
steps: Student 1 does an action and says it. Student 2 repeats it and adds a new one.
The chain grows. The whole row helps if someone forgets.
Reverse the order, or run two chains and compare.
phrases: First I jump, then I turn.
easier: Keep chains to three actions.
harder: Add adverbs: slowly, quickly, carefully.

adaptations.mobility: In Action chain, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Action chain, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Action chain, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

student: Give an order to a friend.
easier: Use single colours and objects.
harder: Combine two conditions: something blue and behind a chair.

name: Moving story
description: Students act each action as they hear a short story.
aim: Understand a story through action (TPR storytelling)
steps: Tell a short story about {focus}. Students act each action as they hear it.
Retell it with changes. Students spot the differences and show them.
In groups, students invent a new story for others to act.
phrases: Then he ran to the cone.
easier: Use five very short sentences.
harder: Students tell the story themselves.

adaptations.mobility: In Moving story, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Moving story, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Moving story, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Information-gap relay
description: A runner brings a route from a card back to the team, which builds it.
aim: Pass information accurately under time pressure
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Teams of 4 to 5 stand at the start line. Each team has a hidden route card at the far end ({card}).
Runner 1 goes to the card, reads it, returns and gives the route in English. The team places cones or draws the route.
A second runner checks by walking it. If it is wrong, the caller repeats it with the correction. Rotate roles.
Final round: teams build their own route for another team. Practise: {pe}.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
student: Runner: go to the card and read it.
Come back. Tell your team the route.
Build the route together. Check it.
easier: Use single-step cards.
harder: Use three-step routes with distractors.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.mobility: In Information-gap relay, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Information-gap relay, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Information-gap relay, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Running dictation
description: Runners read a text on the wall and dictate it to a writer.
aim: Memorise, dictate and check written English
steps: Stick a short text (3 to 5 sentences about {focus}) at the far side of the space.
Runners go to the text, memorise a piece, return and dictate it to the writer in their team.
Teams compare their text with the original and correct it together. Swap roles.
easier: Use one short sentence per run.
harder: Use a longer text with numbers and names.

adaptations.mobility: In Running dictation, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Running dictation, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Running dictation, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Grab the card
description: Teams take turns to grab the card the teacher calls out, aiming to beat the class best.
steps: Spread cards face up at the far end. Teams line up behind a cone.
Call a word or sentence. One runner from each team grabs the matching card and returns.
The team says the sentence in English to score a point for the class best.
easier: Use pictures with words.
harder: Call definitions instead of the words.

adaptations.mobility: In Grab the card, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Grab the card, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Grab the card, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Treasure hunt
description: Teams follow written clues around the space to find the final clue.
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Hide 6 clue cards around the space ({card}). Each team gets its first clue.
A reader reads the clue aloud. The team follows the directions to find the next clue.
Teams rehearse each instruction first (say it, show it or point), use as much English as they can, and may ask the teacher for one hint before moving.
The round ends when every team has read the final clue aloud, and teams cheer each other on. Link it to: {pe}.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
student: Rehearse each instruction, then say it in English as well as you can.
easier: Use picture clues.
harder: Use riddle clues with prepositions and conditionals.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.mobility: In Treasure hunt, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Treasure hunt, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Treasure hunt, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: River crossing
description: Teams cross a taped river using three stepping stones.
aim: Give clear instructions in a problem task
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Mark a river with tape. Each team has 3 hoops or mats as stepping stones.
One team member leads each attempt and gives instructions in English (a card with key phrases helps). Others follow and may ask for repetition. Rotate the leader each attempt.
Teams replan after each attempt, then say what worked and why.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
easier: Show the route on a card first.
harder: Rotate the leader and remove one hoop.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.mobility: In River crossing, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In River crossing, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In River crossing, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Password checkpoint run
description: Each player says the password sentence to pass a checkpoint.
aim: Say a target sentence to pass
steps: Set up checkpoints with cones. Each team has a password sentence about {focus}.
A player says the sentence to the checkpoint guard to continue. If it is not clear, they go back and practise with a partner.
The class goal is to get every member of every team through. Guards rotate.
easier: Use a very short password.
harder: Use a new question each round.

adaptations.mobility: In Password checkpoint run, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Password checkpoint run, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Password checkpoint run, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Penalty shootout questions
description: A shooter answers a question card, then takes a penalty.
aim: Answer in full sentences under mild pressure
steps: Mark a small goal with cones. A shooter takes a question card and answers in a full sentence.
The goalkeeper repeats the answer with different words, then the shooter kicks.
Teams swap roles. Count goals plus correct sentences.
easier: Use yes/no questions.
harder: Use opinion questions that need because.

adaptations.mobility: In Penalty shootout questions, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Penalty shootout questions, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Penalty shootout questions, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Coach and team plan
description: Teams plan a strategy in English, play a short round, then replan.
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Teams plan a strategy in English for 3 minutes, using first, then and we should.
Play a short round using the plan. Link it to: {pe}.
Teams explain what worked, using because and so.
Replan and play again with one change.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
easier: Give a plan frame to fill in.
harder: Add an unexpected rule change mid-round.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.mobility: In Coach and team plan, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Coach and team plan, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Coach and team plan, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Floor-grid routes
description: Pairs walk routes on a taped floor grid from a card.
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Pairs: A holds a route card ({card}) and gives it aloud. B follows it on a floor grid made with tape or desks.
Swap roles with a new card. The pair checks the route against the card.
Each pair builds one new route for the next pair to follow.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
student: A reads the card. Say it in English.
easier: Use one-step cards.
harder: Use routes with obstacles and conditions.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.hearing: In Floor-grid routes, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Eyes-open guide
description: One partner follows spoken directions through a short course.
steps: Set a short, clear route with cones. Partners agree their roles and keep their eyes open. One partner walks slowly while the other gives English directions; either may stop at any time.
Use {cmds}. No touching and no running.
Swap. Change the course and try again.
student: Swap and try a new course.
phrases: You are next to the cone.
easier: Use a very short course.
harder: Use a longer course and limit the words allowed.

name: Pose and describe
description: A reads a pose card; B performs it slowly and holds it.
steps: Pairs get pose cards. A reads the pose instruction and B performs it slowly.
Hold each pose for five breaths while A describes what B is doing.
Swap and make a three-pose flow for another pair.
phrases: She is balancing on one leg.
easier: Use pictures with words.
harder: Add adverbs and precise body parts.

name: Exercise dictation
description: One partner dictates an exercise and number, the other does and writes it.
steps: Pairs have cards with a number and an exercise, for example 8 jumping jacks.
A dictates the card. B does the exercise, counts aloud and writes it.
Swap and check the written cards together.
easier: Use numbers up to 10.
harder: Add frequency words and times.

adaptations.mobility: In Exercise dictation, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Exercise dictation, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Exercise dictation, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Circle commentary
description: Students pass a ball in a circle and describe what is happening.
steps: Students stand in a circle and pass a ball while moving.
The player with the ball describes the action in English, for example I am passing to Sam.
A commentator in the middle repeats the best sentence.
Rotate roles and raise the pace to practise: {pe}.
student: Pass the ball and say what you do.
Listen and repeat the best sentence.
easier: Use a frame: I pass to...
harder: Add questions after each pass.

adaptations.mobility: In Circle commentary, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Circle commentary, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Circle commentary, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Pass and ask
description: Whoever catches the ball asks a question; the next answers.
aim: Ask and answer questions at speed
steps: Teams stand in a line or circle and pass a ball. The receiver asks a question about {focus}.
The next player answers before passing on.
Add a timer for a whole-team score.

name: Music and questions
description: A ball passes in a circle; when the music stops the holder answers.
steps: Students pass a ball or beanbag while music plays. When it stops the holder answers a question card.
Use topics linked to {focus}.
A student may choose a friend to help with the answer.
easier: Use picture cards.
harder: Answer without looking at the card.

name: Catch and say
description: Throw a ball to a friend and say a word from the category.
steps: Stand in a circle. Throw the ball to a friend and say a word from a category (sports, places, directions).
The catcher says a new word and throws on. No repeats.
Change the category when you blow the whistle.
student: Catch and say a new one.
easier: Allow repeats at first.
harder: Ask for sentences, not words.

name: Language stations
description: Four movement stations, each with a small speaking, listening or reading task.
steps: Set up 4 stations. Each has a movement and a micro-task: say, listen, read, act.
Groups rotate every 4 minutes on a signal.
A station leader checks the target language at each stop.
Whole class: each group reports one thing it learned.
student: Rotate when you hear the signal.
easier: Make tasks picture-based.
harder: Add a challenge card at each station.

name: Press conference
description: Reporters interview an athlete or coach.
aim: Ask and answer questions in role
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
One student is an athlete or coach. The others are reporters with question cards.
Reporters stand in a line, ask one question each and listen to the answer.
Swap roles. Add a follow-up question to extend the answer.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
easier: Provide question cards.
harder: Remove the cards and use follow-ups only.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.mobility: In Press conference, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Press conference, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Press conference, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

description: Groups build a frozen picture; the class describes it.

Groups unfreeze for 5 seconds of action, then freeze again.

Groups unfreeze for 5 seconds of action, then freeze again. Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support. name: Movement bingo
description: Students complete bingo cards by doing the called actions.
steps: Each student has a bingo card with actions or sentences.
Call items. Students do the action and mark the square.
The first to complete a line says Bingo! and leads the next round.
easier: Use pictures instead of words.
harder: Students call the items in sentences.

adaptations.mobility: In Movement bingo, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Movement bingo, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Movement bingo, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

description: Pairs roll a dice; each number matches an action.
steps: Pairs roll a dice. Each number matches an action card (1 jump, 2 spin, 3 clap).

easier: Use pictures with words.
harder: Add a second dice for the number of times.

name: Move and speak board game
description: Groups roll, move and do what the square says.
aim: Mix movement and speaking in one game
steps: Groups of 4 use a floor or table board. Roll, move, and do what the square says.
Action squares need a movement; question squares need an answer in English.
The first player to reach the end says one sentence about the journey.
easier: Remove question squares.
harder: Add a challenge square that needs two sentences.

name: Seated relay
description: A card or message passes along rows of seated students.
aim: Pass and say messages in a small space
steps: Pairs or rows remain seated with clear space for comfortable arm movement.
Pass a pictured message or an accessible communication device along the row. The final learner selects the matching picture; compare it with the original.
Rotate speaker and checker responsibilities without moving seats. No writing is required.
easier: Use short words.
harder: Use longer sentences and compare the result.
outcome: Identify the original message at the end of the chain.

adaptations.hearing: In Seated relay, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Classroom mystery trail
description: Pairs follow clues hidden around the classroom.
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Hide clue cards around the classroom. Pairs follow directions to the next one.
Directions use {cmds}. No running.
The final clue is a task. Pairs perform it for the class.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
easier: Use picture clues.
harder: Use riddles and negative directions.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.hearing: In Classroom mystery trail, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Invent a game
description: Groups design a PE game that practises the language focus.
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Groups design a short PE game that practises {focus}. They write the rules in English.
They teach the game to another group using only English and demonstration.
Groups give two stars and a wish.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
student: Give two stars and a wish.
easier: Give a rules template.
harder: Add a scoring system and a safety rule.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

adaptations.mobility: In Invent a game, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Invent a game, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Invent a game, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Pre-match talk
description: Coaches deliver a pre-match talk, then the team plays using the plan.
steps: Set a genuine gap: give partners different clues or choices that they cannot see on each other’s cards. Agree what result they will compare at the end.
Teams plan tactics for a simple game and a motivating speech.
Coaches deliver the talk, then the team plays 3 minutes using the plan.
After the game, the coach explains what worked using because.
Report the result, compare it with the hidden source or agreed criteria, and discuss one repair. Learners may use any English they have; suggested phrases are support.
easier: Provide a speech frame.
harder: Ask for a second plan after a change of rule.
outcome: Agree, reconstruct or identify a result and check it against the source or agreed criteria.
gap: information, reasoning or opinion gap (teacher sets the hidden clue or choice)

name: Opposite day
description: A has a secret opposite-action rule. B must discover it and recreate a two-action pattern.
steps: A sees a secret rule: up means down; open means closed. Model safe arm movements only.
B requests two actions, observes the responses and chooses the hidden rule from two picture choices.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Compare the chosen rule with the secret. Swap rule-maker and detective.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Discover the hidden movement rule.

adaptations.mobility: Keep opposite day at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For opposite day, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For opposite day, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Tray of commands
description: Partners hold different views of a token tray and must make the trays match.
steps: A secretly arranges three objects or drawn tokens on a tray. B starts with the same objects in a different order.
Without showing the tray, A directs B to move, place or turn the tokens. B asks for repetition.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Reveal both trays, compare the arrangements and fix differences. Swap roles.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Reproduce a hidden arrangement.

adaptations.mobility: Keep tray of commands at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For tray of commands, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For tray of commands, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Signal crew
description: Teams devise a shared signal system and use it to move a token to a destination.
steps: Choose a start and a secret destination on a small tabletop map. Give each learner one signal to contribute.
Agree commands for moving a token. One partner gives the commands while another uses only the agreed signals.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Check the final destination, repair an unclear signal and exchange roles.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Deliver a token to the agreed destination.

adaptations.mobility: Keep signal crew at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For signal crew, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For signal crew, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Pattern makers
description: One partner knows a pattern; another reconstructs it through spoken action choices.
steps: A makes a secret pattern of two or three safe hand actions. B has two possible picture sequences.
B asks A for commands and performs them. A gives feedback that helps B choose a sequence.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
B selects and performs the matching pattern. Reveal the source and swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Identify and reproduce a secret action pattern.

adaptations.mobility: Keep pattern makers at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For pattern makers, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For pattern makers, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Parcel partners
description: Partners exchange instructions to deliver a paper parcel to its hidden home.
steps: Give A a secret home symbol and B a token with two possible matching destinations.
A gives commands to move the parcel one step at a time. B checks uncertain steps aloud.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Reveal the home symbol and check delivery. Change the home and swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Deliver a parcel to its matching home.

adaptations.mobility: Keep parcel partners at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For parcel partners, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For parcel partners, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Build a signal
description: Partners test competing commands and choose the clearest signal for a shared goal.
steps: Show two possible gestures for one safe action. Partners each privately choose a preferred signal.
Explain or demonstrate the choices, then agree which command and gesture will help a new partner act.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Invite another pair to test the signal; revise it if the action is unclear.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Agree and test a usable class signal.

name: Giving and following commands · movement preview
description: Rehearse the coming task with slow, comfortable actions and a visible stop signal.
steps: Teacher models two focus phrases with a comfortable action or a tabletop token.
Partners take one turn each: listen or look, respond, then request a repeat if needed.
Preview the main task’s goal. Speech is invited when ready, never required before comprehension.
easier: Offer two choices and a gesture.
harder: At B1/B2, rehearse clarification and negotiation; keep this preview brief.

adaptations.mobility: In Giving and following commands · movement preview, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Giving and following commands · movement preview, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Giving and following commands · movement preview, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Maze master
description: A knows the exit; B moves a token through a desk-sized maze.
steps: Sketch a simple maze with two possible exits. A secretly marks the correct exit.
A gives directions without pointing to the exit. B moves a token and asks for clarification.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Compare the finish with the hidden exit, repair the route and swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Find the hidden exit.

adaptations.mobility: Keep maze master at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For maze master, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For maze master, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Robot and programmer
description: A programmer guides a partner or token to a hidden destination.
steps: Make a small grid with drawn objects. The programmer privately chooses one destination.
The programmer gives instructions; the robot moves a token or walks slowly on a clear grid. Eyes remain open.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
The robot identifies the destination. Check it, change the destination and swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Reach and identify the secret destination.

adaptations.mobility: Keep robot and programmer at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For robot and programmer, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For robot and programmer, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Lost kit desk
description: Partners hold different information about where equipment belongs.
steps: A sees a layout of kit locations. B receives three kit tokens and an empty matching map.
B asks where each item belongs; A explains locations without revealing the layout.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Place the tokens, compare maps and correct mismatches. Swap map-holder.

name: Choose the route
description: Partners combine separate route information to find a workable path.
steps: Draw two short routes. A knows which path is clear; B knows the destination.
Exchange directions and blockage information. Agree a route and trace it with a finger or token.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Check that the path reaches the destination without crossing the marked blockage. Swap information.

harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Agree a route that satisfies both clues.

name: Delivery route
description: Partners combine an address clue and a route clue to deliver a token.
steps: One partner privately sees the delivery symbol. The other knows which route reaches each symbol.
Ask and answer about destinations and directions until a delivery route is agreed.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Move the parcel token, reveal the address and check delivery. Exchange roles.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Deliver a token using two different clues.

adaptations.hearing: For delivery route, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

steps: Teacher models two focus phrases with a comfortable action or a tabletop token.

easier: Offer two choices and a gesture.

adaptations.hearing: In Giving and following directions · movement preview, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Photo finish describe
description: An observer describes a frozen action so a partner can identify it.
steps: A secretly chooses one of three teacher-demonstrated poses. Use no camera or personal photographs.
A describes the chosen pose while B selects its matching picture or performs a possible match.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Compare the choice with the secret pose, explain one difference and swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Identify the hidden pose.

adaptations.mobility: Keep photo finish describe at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For photo finish describe, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For photo finish describe, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Statue garden
description: Partners identify a secret statue using its action and position.
steps: Three volunteers choose comfortable poses, seated or standing. A privately selects one as the target.
B asks about actions and locations; A describes without naming or pointing to the target.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
B selects the statue and explains the clue. Change the target and rotate roles.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Find a statue from descriptive clues.

adaptations.mobility: Keep statue garden at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For statue garden, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For statue garden, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Commentary match
description: A listener selects the correct replay using a partner’s commentary.
steps: A privately chooses one of two safe hand-action sequences. B knows both possible sequences.
A describes the chosen action as a volunteer performs behind a small screen or away from B’s view.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
B selects the matching sequence; reveal the performance and compare. Swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Match commentary to a hidden action sequence.

adaptations.mobility: Keep commentary match at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For commentary match, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For commentary match, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Pose gallery curators
description: Pairs agree which of two descriptions best matches a hidden pose.
steps: A views a simple pose while B receives two possible picture descriptions from the teacher.
A describes the pose. B proposes the best match and asks about any missing detail.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Reveal the picture, agree a gallery label and swap roles.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Choose a matching gallery picture.

adaptations.mobility: Keep pose gallery curators at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For pose gallery curators, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For pose gallery curators, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

description: Rehearse the coming task with slow, comfortable actions and a visible stop signal.
steps: Teacher models two focus phrases with a comfortable action or a tabletop token.

Preview the main task’s goal. Speech is invited when ready, never required before comprehension.
easier: Offer two choices and a gesture.
harder: At B1/B2, rehearse clarification and negotiation; keep this preview brief.

adaptations.hearing: In Describing what people are doing · movement preview, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Human storyboard
description: Partners reconstruct a short hidden story from separately held picture clues.
steps: Show partners different parts of a three-picture movement story, without written text.
Describe or mime the separate events, then agree their order. Use first and then when ready.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Perform the ordered story and compare it with the teacher’s model. Change roles.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Reconstruct a picture story.

adaptations.mobility: Keep human storyboard at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For human storyboard, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For human storyboard, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Course narration
description: Partners reconstruct a tabletop movement course from ordered spoken clues.
steps: A privately sees a two- or three-stop course; B receives the same landmark tokens out of order.
A narrates the route while B places the tokens in sequence. Ask again when the order is unclear.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Trace or slowly walk the agreed order, compare with the source and swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Reconstruct the ordered course.

adaptations.mobility: Keep course narration at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For course narration, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For course narration, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

steps: A sees the start of a short replay and B sees the finish. Give both a middle-step choice.
Exchange what happened and agree which middle action connects the replay.

Perform the whole sequence, compare the middle step with the model and change roles.

easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Repair a mixed-up replay.

name: Rhythm puzzle
description: Partners combine two hidden halves of a hand rhythm.
steps: Teacher demonstrates the first half of a four-beat rhythm to A and the second half to B.
Describe or softly tap each half and agree the full order. Use a visual beat cue instead of sound if preferred.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Perform the full rhythm together and compare with the model. Swap halves.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Combine two halves of a rhythm.

adaptations.mobility: Keep rhythm puzzle at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For rhythm puzzle, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For rhythm puzzle, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Routine builders
description: Partners combine different choices to agree a two-step movement routine.
steps: Each partner privately chooses one comfortable hand or arm movement. Both movements must fit the routine.
Share the choices and agree which goes first and which comes next. Let each person suggest an order.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Perform the agreed routine, check that both choices appear and explain the order.

description: Partners use different views of a pretend incident to agree a fair restart.
steps: Demonstrate a non-contact pretend game moment. A knows the last touch; B knows the agreed boundary rule.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Agree a restart that fits both clues, demonstrate it with tokens and explain why.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Agree a restart using both pieces of information.

harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.

name: Fair roles council
description: Partners choose a role rotation that gives everyone a meaningful turn.
steps: Show two or three role pictures for a small team task. Each partner privately chooses a preferred role.
Compare preferences and negotiate a first round and a swap so both contribute.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Act the rotation with tokens and verify that everyone gets a choice and a turn.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Agree a fair role rotation.

adaptations.mobility: Keep fair roles council at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For fair roles council, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For fair roles council, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

description: Partners adapt a shared token route after an unexpected change.
steps: Agree a simple tabletop route. A privately receives a new blockage and B receives a new destination.
Reveal the change through spoken clues and negotiate a replacement route.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Test the route, explain one revision and confirm that both new conditions are met.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Repair a plan after two changed conditions.

adaptations.hearing: For rescue the plan, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Planning and suggesting (team strategy) · movement preview
description: Rehearse the coming task with slow, comfortable actions and a visible stop signal.
steps: Teacher models two focus phrases with a comfortable action or a tabletop token.
Partners take one turn each: listen or look, respond, then request a repeat if needed.
Preview the main task’s goal. Speech is invited when ready, never required before comprehension.
easier: Offer two choices and a gesture.
harder: At B1/B2, rehearse clarification and negotiation; keep this preview brief.

adaptations.mobility: In Planning and suggesting (team strategy) · movement preview, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Planning and suggesting (team strategy) · movement preview, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Planning and suggesting (team strategy) · movement preview, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.

name: Hot seat athlete
description: Partners ask questions to identify a fictional athlete’s secret preference.
steps: Teacher gives A a private picture choice for a fictional athlete’s favourite action. Avoid personal learner information.
B asks yes/no questions and uses the answers to choose the matching picture.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Reveal the picture, check the choice and swap interviewer and athlete.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Identify a fictional athlete’s preference.

adaptations.mobility: Keep hot seat athlete at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For hot seat athlete, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For hot seat athlete, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Yes/no line
description: Partners combine yes/no answers to locate a hidden picture.
steps: Arrange three action pictures on a table. A secretly chooses one. Responses can use pointing, a voice or a device.
B asks yes/no questions to eliminate pictures and moves a token towards a final choice.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Reveal the secret picture, compare and swap roles. No learner must move to a public yes/no position.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Identify a hidden action picture.

adaptations.mobility: Keep yes/no line at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For yes/no line, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For yes/no line, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Partner finder
description: Learners ask questions to find the matching fictional role card.
steps: Give each partner a private pair of picture choices; exactly one choice matches across the pair.
Ask questions about the choices without showing them and agree a possible match.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
Reveal the pictures and check the shared choice. Exchange one picture and try again.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Find the shared picture.

adaptations.mobility: Keep partner finder at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For partner finder, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For partner finder, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: The missing rule
description: Partners ask questions to discover a hidden movement-game rule.
steps: A privately chooses a rule picture: one clap or two, left or right. B sees the available choices.
B asks questions and tests a safe hand action to narrow down the rule.

Movement application: act out the chosen route, pose or sequence with slow, comfortable movement in a teacher-checked space. A seated arm-action or reachable token version has the same information and decision-making goal. Do not turn this into a speed contest.
State or show the discovered rule, reveal the source and swap.
student: Ask or show what you need.
easier: Use two picture choices, model one turn, accept a gesture or one word and allow thinking time.
harder: Use four choices, keep clues hidden, ask for reasons and negotiate a revision without a sentence script.
outcome: Discover the hidden rule.

adaptations.mobility: Keep the missing rule at a reachable table. Move tokens or use comfortable upper-body actions; swap clue-holder and decision-maker so both roles have equal status.
adaptations.vision: For the missing rule, describe each picture or use distinct tactile objects. Keep the hidden information private by telling the clue-holder quietly; do not rely on colour alone.
adaptations.hearing: For the missing rule, show each instruction and the stop signal, face the partner and use readable picture cues or a communication device. Keep turns visible.

name: Asking and answering questions · movement preview
description: Rehearse the coming task with slow, comfortable actions and a visible stop signal.
steps: Teacher models two focus phrases with a comfortable action or a tabletop token.
Partners take one turn each: listen or look, respond, then request a repeat if needed.
Preview the main task’s goal. Speech is invited when ready, never required before comprehension.
easier: Offer two choices and a gesture.
harder: At B1/B2, rehearse clarification and negotiation; keep this preview brief.

adaptations.mobility: In Asking and answering questions · movement preview, replace travel with a reachable token route or comfortable upper-body action. Rotate the information-giving and checking roles, with the same decision-making responsibility.
adaptations.vision: In Asking and answering questions · movement preview, describe the setup before play, use high-contrast or tactile markers and speak every visual signal. Offer a consistent partner and an eyes-open route.
adaptations.hearing: In Asking and answering questions · movement preview, face partners, model each step and pair every sound cue with a visible signal. Use picture instructions or a communication device.
